name: EPRI: The Electric Power Research Institute's AI Programmes for the Power Sector
title: EPRI: The Electric Power Research Institute's AI Programmes for the Power Sector
answer: EPRI's website sets out the institute's AI work for the electricity sector, including SAFERai.power, launched on August 6, 2026 to give utilities and technology providers tools, evidence and guardrails for scaling AI responsibly as it moves from pilots to deployment. It also describes Flex MOSAIC and DCFlex for large load flexibility, the Open Power AI Consortium, and AI-assisted nuclear inspection.

sections.body: This is the homepage of the Electric Power Research Institute, the utility-backed research organisation known as EPRI. The page presents EPRI's AI-related initiatives, announcements and resources rather than a single report or dataset. It carries dated announcements from 2026, including SAFERai.power on August 6 and executive leadership changes on July 28, alongside descriptions of ongoing programmes and an episode of the EPRI Current podcast featuring Exelon.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page describes several EPRI efforts that touch on artificial intelligence in the power sector. SAFERai.power is a collaborative initiative announced on August 6, 2026, intended to equip utilities and technology providers with the tools, evidence and guardrails needed to scale AI responsibly, as the technology moves from pilot projects to real-world deployment and creates a need for trusted, consistent methods to evaluate operational risk. Flex MOSAIC is a classification framework defining how large power users can flex their demand to support the grid, and DCFlex provides a technology neutral, uniform structure for describing and evaluating large load flexibility, turning technical capability into actionable grid response for what EPRI calls an AI-driven economy. The cross-sector Open Power AI Consortium aims to evolve the electric sector by leveraging advanced AI to innovate how electricity is made, moved and used, driving solutions that enhance operational efficiency, resiliency and reliability, deploy emerging technologies and reduce costs while improving the customer experience. EPRI's nuclear inspection performance demonstration facility, which has set inspection reliability standards for more than 30 years, is evolving to support AI-assisted inspections and advanced reactor designs. An EPRI Current podcast episode with Exelon covers climate-ready grid planning, including the role of AI and data in risk management, alongside EPRI's Climate READi and Exelon's Climate Change Investment Initiative. EPRI also announced leadership changes to address emerging power sector needs as AI and digital technologies drive rapidly growing energy use, which it calls the most significant shift in energy research in a generation.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The page gives two dates, August 6, 2026 for the SAFERai.power announcement and July 28, 2026 for the leadership changes, and states that EPRI's nuclear inspection performance demonstration facility has set the standard for inspection reliability for more than 30 years. It offers no quantitative results, cost figures or performance data for the AI programmes themselves.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in the energy industry would use this page to track where the sector's shared research layer is heading. EPRI is utility-backed, so its programmes indicate what utilities collectively consider worth funding and standardising. SAFERai.power speaks directly to the gap between AI pilots and deployment by proposing common methods for evaluating operational risk, while Flex MOSAIC and DCFlex address the demand-side flexibility that growing AI-driven electricity use makes more urgent. The Open Power AI Consortium and the nuclear inspection work show the same organisation applying AI across both operations and generation.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Energy

sections.body: This is a homepage, so it summarises initiatives rather than reporting their methods, results or membership terms. Several items are announcements of intent, including SAFERai.power and the leadership changes, with no detail on how the tools, evidence or guardrails will be produced or who participates. The page is promotional in tone and gives no independent evaluation of the programmes it describes.
